    Breaking: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).
    • It has been revealed that the list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration.
    • The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).

    It has been revealed that the list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”.

    The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

    Fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

    Recent findings suggest that given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the upcoming year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

    According to recent reports, the budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

    As part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

    The key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission blueprint that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test concerns.

    NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain problems for key hardware components.

    “Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”.

    Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them quickly or reliably.

    Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them quickly.

    • Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.

    The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.

    Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.

    By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the firm tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.

    According to recent reports, in its announcement, Amazon stated it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the firm offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.

    One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.

    Sources indicate that annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.

    In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, remarked the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”.

    It has been revealed that amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, mentioned on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”.

    HIV infections could rise amid aid cuts, UN warns

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.
    • "The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency noted in its annual global revision.
    • Industry observers note that AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.

    "The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency noted in its annual global revision.

    Industry observers note that AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades. According to the organization, this was made possible by broader access to treatment and improvements in the quality of care programs.

    Recent findings suggest that the virus claimed roughly 570,000 lives globally in 2025. This means almost 1,600 people died everyday. In comparison, this figure was 600,000 in 2024 and 1.3 million in 2010.

    Based on data from 172 countries, the agency estimated that 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2025, of whom 32.1 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment.

    Industry observers note that the wider use of antiretroviral medication also reduces the risk of HIV transmission, the organization stated. It estimates that 1.2 million people contracted HIV in 2025, down from 1.3 million the year before. The peak in 1994 saw 3.5 million.

    "HIV, which was once a death sentence, has become a manageable health condition for millions of people thanks to life-saving HIV medicines," said UNAIDS.

    Despite the encouraging data so far, cuts to international funding have hampered efforts to fight HIV, the agency warned.

    HIV programs faced an 18-percent decrease in international financing over the past year, remarked UNAIDS.

    "Funding losses have destabilized HIV programs worldwide, coinciding with a wider contraction in official development assistance over the years," it said.

    Although the United States remains the largest international donor for HIV programs, its contributions dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    After dismantling USAID, the world's largest foreign aid agency, last year, the Donald Trump administration has sought to replace decades of aid with new bilateral deals.

    "The impact of the United States government funding cuts has been especially dramatic given the reliance of many countries on its support for core HIV programs," stated UNAIDS.

    Meanwhile disbursements from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria dropped by 13% in 2025.

    "We are on the cusp of ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global ​health – and just when we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights is ​threatening to take away our gains," Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told ​Reuters.

    In a recent development, "We haven't ‌got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs of reversals," she added.

    Byanyima predicted that data released in 2027 would begin to reflect a rise in upcoming HIV infections.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024.

    A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

    Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

    It has been revealed that ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

    This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

    In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

    At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers noted.

    There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

    On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

    "We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.

    "The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately.".

    Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

    "Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," mentioned Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

    Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

    In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

    Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

    Sources indicate that since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

    In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.

    Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

    According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.

    Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it claims.

    • Sources indicate that pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one fresh feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to.
    • The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
    • Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta unveiled a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one fresh feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.

    The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.

    Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta unveiled a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.

    WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.

    But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.

    Recent findings suggest that this problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to owners under 18.

    Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into consumers’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.

    Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the consumers themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.

    It has been revealed that the new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

    #81622. No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (505 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that car buyers in New York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year.
    • “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car.
    • In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that car buyers in New York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year.

    “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in Latest York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor stated.

    In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee.

    Recent findings suggest that we end users might not like having to open our wallets each month, but the capital markets sure do, and car companies love making the capital markets happy. Which is why there has been such a push toward connected vehicles. Remote start and predictive maintenance alerts are nice, but your regular payments to the car organization—plus any data of yours it can sell—is the goal.

    Recent findings suggest that some automakers have gone even further. Infamously, BMW and its heated seats. Like the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit, it’s a fact half-remembered; BMW North America never tried such a thing, just in countries like South Korea and the UK, and in 2023 BMW’s board said that subscriptions would only be for software-related features from then on.

    New York’s press release mentions heated seats but also calls out a number of other modern tech features: “enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.”.

    But the way the actual law is written appears to leave a rather large loophole, at least to these eyes.

    S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

    Industry observers note that A heated seat might not have “an ongoing cost,” but the maps and databases that enable “enhanced navigation” and “hands-free driving” systems definitely do, as these need to be constantly updated. A regular cadence of software updates also generates an ongoing cost to an OEM, arguably. And car companies pay for plenty of lawyers who really love to argue.

    And so, while experiments like BMW’s seat heater subscription won’t be allowed in the state, the new rule might still allow for plenty of ongoing fees for services like OnStar or Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro system we tested recently.

    Latest Update: How to make your USB-C cables last longer

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Simple handling, cleaning and storage habits keep USB-C cables working longer and help you avoid costly replacements.
    • USB-C cables have become crucial in everyday life; they power our phones, laptops, gaming controllers and many other things.
    • It has been revealed that although there's no fixed number for how long a USB-C cable should last, the USB-Implementers Forum (USB-IF) set in stone that the durability of the platform should last for 10,000 mating cycles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Simple handling, cleaning and storage habits keep USB-C cables working longer and help you avoid costly replacements.

    USB-C cables have become crucial in everyday life; they power our phones, laptops, gaming controllers and many other things. But unfortunately, these cables seem to have a knack for going bad at the worst times. Thankfully, that can be mitigated. With a few simple steps, you can make your USB-C cable last much longer.

    It has been revealed that although there's no fixed number for how long a USB-C cable should last, the USB-Implementers Forum (USB-IF) set in stone that the durability of the platform should last for 10,000 mating cycles. So the connector is usually not the matter when a cable goes bad. Most times, it's the cord itself, and the weak point of most cables is where the cord meets the connector. Everyday habits often do most of the damage. One of the most common ones is yanking the cord to unplug instead of the connector, and sharply folding the cord is another. Thankfully, extending your USB-C cable's lifespan is pretty straightforward. Careful handling, proper storage, regularly cleaning your connectors and ports and simply ignoring $2 low-quality cables on Amazon go a long way to making your USB-C cable last longer.

    There's a correct way to handle USB-C cables, and it doesn't involve yanking. When unplugging, never pull the cord. Instead, grip the plug head. Yanking causes the internal wires to break and gradually pull away from the connector. You should also avoid twisting and bending the cable when it's plugged in. Instead, gently loop it without making any sharp bends or hard creases. Keep cables off the floor and away from chair wheels or foot traffic, which can crush internal wires while everything looks fine on the outside. Extreme temperatures are another threat. Exposure to heat can break down the cable's outer layer, while cold makes it brittle and prone to cracking.

    Finally, your USB-C cables and ports can easily pick up lint, dust and debris, which can cause loose connections or accelerate wear. Cleaning them is easier than you think: all you need is compressed air. Never use sharp or metal objects, as they can scratch the contact pins or short circuit the device. Hold the compressed air can upright about 15 cm away and spray short blasts into the port, tilting the connector at different angles to dislodge trapped dirt. Just be thankful that smart phones only use USB-C ports these days, as no one liked cleaning the myriad of proprietary ports they used to have, especially the Motorola 17-pin CE bus connector. Just be thankful that smartphones only use USB-C ports these days. No one liked cleaning proprietary ports, especially the Motorola 17-pin CE bus connector, which was giant compared to USB-C.

    There is a proper way and place to keep your USB-C cable, and neglecting it will cut short your cable's lifespan without you even knowing it. When storing or moving, first, unplug the cable so the connectors aren't under strain. Next, coil the cable in a loose loop about the size of your palm, avoiding sharp twists and bends. Making a knot or wrapping it tight around the charging brick can damage and break internal wires. Also, don't leave them to get tangled. The force of untangling actually damages your USB-C cable due to stressing the wires.

    In a recent development, A good idea if you keep lots of cables in the same place, is to secure the cluster with a Velcro strap or silicone organizer. Avoid using rubber bands and twist ties on your cable, unlike Velcro straps they create pressure points which can damage the cable over time. Lastly, your USB-C cable prefers to be kept in a dry and cool environment. Heat accelerates wear and humidity can cause corrosion inside the connectors especially if your USB-C cable isn't waterproof.

    Recent findings suggest that the best way to make your USB-C cable last longer is to skip the $2 cables and buy quality ones right from the start. Look for cables from reputable brands with reinforced strain relief, a braided or thick outer layer and USB-IF certification. These typically last longer thanks to their higher build quality, while certification ensures the cable actually does what it advertises.

    It has been revealed that A cable's length can also affect its performance. For example, USB4 cables have a recommended maximum length of just 0.8 meters (about 31 inches). Go beyond that, and concerns with power delivery, signal degradation and slower data transfers start to appear.

    According to recent reports, once a cable develops cracks, fraying, exposed wires or bent connectors, it's time to replace it. The longer you keep using that damaged cable, the greater the risk that a few dollars' worth of replacement turns into a much more serious problem. According to a report from The Republic, investigators believe a frayed charging cord started a 2017 house fire causing an estimated $50,000 to $70,000 in damage. Do not attempt to fix a broken cord yourself; the Electrical Safety Foundation International strongly advises against DIY cable repairs. Buying a replacement is always the safer fix.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Andrei Chibis's wife rejects the allegations and he is expected to appear in court on Thursday.

    The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.

    Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; Â£9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.

    Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.

    In a recent development, he denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis noted "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".

    In a post on social media, she said her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now.".

    Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.

    Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

    The port of Murmansk is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

    Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.

    However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

    The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.

    Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.

    According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.

    He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

    No American company, including NVIDIA, can sell technologies to Megaspeed without a license from the federal government.

    The US Commerce Department has added Megaspeed, the Singaporean manufacturer at the center of the NVIDIA scandal, to its "entity list." The addition means no American company, including NVIDIA, can sell technologies such as AI chips to Megaspeed or its affiliates without a license from the federal government.

    The move comes just a day after NVIDIA restored Jensen Huang as its CEO and president following direct intervention from President Donald Trump. Huang had resigned from his position on November 12 after reports surfaced that he had cultivated multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving a former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy. Noted suspected spy, Alice Huang (no relation to the NVIDIA CEO), took a controlling stake in Megaspeed in 2023 before leaving the tech giant in August 2025. In a joint statement issued last week alongside the Department of Justice, the Commerce Department said it had begun investigating Megaspeed in 2024, and that NVIDIA had placed the cloud computing firm on its own "no sell" list in June 2025. China has denied the allegations Alice Huang was a spy.

    On Monday, NVIDIA's board of directors mentioned it had voted unanimously to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO. Just days earlier, Harvey Jones, the chair of NVIDIA's board of directors, said the tech giant did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." On late Sunday evening, the board met to vote on Huang's reinstatement, with President Trump calling into the meeting. Following reporting from Semafor, Trump confirmed he influenced the board's decision. "And I convinced them," Trump told CNBC. "I made the deal.".

    Congolese rebels said they had targeted a warplane preparing to bomb the town of Minembwe.

    The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.

    The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.

    On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a plane of the same type that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.

    Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.

    On Tuesday, the FRN remarked the plane they had shot down was a Cessna 208, which had been "converted into a light attack aircraft" enabling it "to carry and launch precision-guided bombs and missiles".

    Its wreckage now lies 10km (6 miles) from Minembwe, a rebel statement said, adding that a Ugandan and South African "mercenaries" had been captured.

    The BBC has not independently verified the rebel claim, or whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one the rebels say they shot down.

    South Africa's government has not commented, while Uganda's military has denied any involvement.

    What's the fighting in DR Congo all about?

    How former President Kabila became FRN rebel leader.

    Recent findings suggest that A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company.".

    The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.

    Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".

    Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.

    In a recent development, in the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.

    He and the alleged South African pilot are remarked to be the only other survivors.

    South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".

    "Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.

    Sources indicate that in 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.

    The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.

    In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.

    The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.

    Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.

    Over the weekend, medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.

    The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

    The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

    Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is.
    • That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV.
    • So, for the firm’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

    That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

    So, for the firm’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.

    According to recent reports, that EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.

    For Porsche’s latest Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

    It has been revealed that porsche isn’t saying how big the new roadster’s battery is in terms of charge capacity, only that its size was chosen to balance range and weight. We also don’t have an idea of rated range, charging speed, nor battery composition, but I can say the battery pack is based on an 800 V architecture like the electric Macan, so hopefully we can expect charging performance that at least matches that SUV’s 270 kW.

    In a recent development, the latest Boxster also shares a motor with the Macan. Porsche is not quoting any specs yet, but it puts out about 500 hp (370 kW) to the rear wheels on the Macan Turbo. You can place your bets on whether the Boxster application will result in more or less power. I would take the over, but regardless, it’s enough to sprint this electric roadster to 62 mph (100 km/h) in under 3.0 seconds, making it the quickest Boxster ever.

    But it’s also the largest and heaviest. I was told the new Boxster’s curb weight will be somewhere in the ballpark of a current-generation 911, so in the region of 3,300 to 3,700 pounds (roughly 1,500 to 1,700 kg), meaning it has gained at least a few hundred pounds. That’s light for an EV but heavy for a roadster. Its wheelbase has grown accordingly.

    Recent findings suggest that you can absolutely feel that on the road. The 718 just doesn’t have the same buzzy eagerness as the latest 718 Boxster or Cayman. But that doesn’t mean it’s less fun to drive. In fact, I think most people would say it’s much more fun. Nearly doubling the old car’s base power output will do that.

    Industry observers note that this car, though, is about a lot more than acceleration. It still turns and handles incredibly well, borrowing much of its suspension, steering, and even chassis from the current-generation 911. Few would call a 911 a boring car, and the 718 is a step more aggressive even than that coupe.

    It has been revealed that that’s in part thanks to the response afforded by the electric powertrain, which isn’t saddled by the lazy throttle application caused by turbochargers and modern emission regulations. It’s sharper even than the latest 911 GTS, which required a trick electrically assisted turbocharger plus a battery and electric motor to bring the EV feel to a car driven by internal combustion.

    To bring some of the charm of internal combustion to an EV, Porsche followed in the footsteps of the Hyundai Ioniq 5N by adding synthesized shifting and engine noises to the mix. Many cringe at the thought of an EV wailing unnecessarily, but having driven many battery-powered machines that make gas-powered noises, I can say with assurance that they always dial up the fun factor.

    It has been revealed that what they often lack is authenticity. Porsche sampled the sound of what its engineers determined was the sweetest-sounding 718: the 981-generation Boxster GTS. The new 718 Boxster replicates both that car’s 3.4 L flat-six and its seven-speed dual-clutch transmission, controlled by the paddles behind the steering wheel.

    It has been revealed that enable the system, which Porsche calls E-Shift, then put the Boxster into launch control, and you’re in for a bit of a show: The car not only sounds like it’s bouncing off of a rev limiter, but the car itself actually shakes. It does this by pulsing the electric motor, vibrating in much the same way that the original Harley-Davidson Livewire did.

    Lift off the brake and the Boxster blasts forward, again doing the sprint to 60 in less than 3 seconds. All the while, the pretend engine is screaming and running through its mock gears, either automatically or at your command with the paddles. In manual mode, the car will hit that artificial rev limiter and abruptly stop accelerating, so you’d better be quick to grab that next gear.

    This whole system is there to add a greater sense of emotion to the car, but it does serve a practical purpose. Slinging the 718 around the tight, twisty circuit at the Los Angeles Porsche Experience Center, I was better able to judge my speed through corners by listening to the pretend engine that sounded all the world like it was spinning happily behind my head.

    Don’t like it? Press the blue button on the steering wheel and it all goes away, but I have a feeling most people will want it on, at least when they’re driving for fun. They will certainly want it on when cruising into their local Cars & Coffee, since you can hear the sound outside the car as well as on the inside.

    Cruising is better in the upcoming 718 than the older model as well. Its adaptive suspension, dialed down to Normal mode, handles concrete separation joints on the highway and bumpy roads without glitch.

    And it offers something extremely rare on the EV scene: true drop-top motoring. The top folds itself down in somewhere around 10 seconds, tucking itself neatly on top of that battery pack. It also offers reasonable practicality, with a frunk in the nose plus a decently wide if shallow trunk out back. Both are roughly big enough to handle a carry-on suitcase or a couple of backpacks. That’s about it, though. There’s effectively no room behind the seats.

    Sources indicate that so, from a lifestyle perspective, it’s a bit more flexible and a bit more comfortable than the previous-generation Boxster, and from a power and aggression standpoint, it’s on another planet. Still, there’s no hiding that increase in weight and wheelbase. This truly feels like a cross-breed between a Boxster and a Carrera, which will disappoint some purists, but if you had to pick a pair of parents for a latest model, you could do a lot worse than those two.

    #81608. Industry News: Use this built-in Windows tool to find PC stability issues

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (732 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Use this built-in Windows tool to find PC stability issues

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An unstable PC can be a nightmare to diagnose.
    • Recent findings suggest that introduced with Windows Vista back in 2008, Windows Reliability Monitor is a convenient way to check all of your computer's logged events.
    • Windows Reliability Monitor is an easy application to use, although accessing the program itself can be a little tricky.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This tool is a great alternative to Event Viewer.

    An unstable PC can be a nightmare to diagnose. Figuring out what's causing a blue screen or a driver crash can take hours if you're digging through event logs and checking for faulty applications. Thankfully, Windows has a suite of troubleshooting programs built specifically to help people diagnose system concerns. Most people know about Performance Monitor and Event Viewer, but arguably the best tool to start a troubleshooting session is the long-forgotten Windows Reliability Monitor.

    Recent findings suggest that introduced with Windows Vista back in 2008, Windows Reliability Monitor is a convenient way to check all of your computer's logged events. This includes crashed drivers, failed applications and other system health concerns you might not otherwise notice. It even gives a stability score to help inexperienced users diagnose stability issues, although that score can be somewhat misleading. It's a great tool to use when your PC starts experiencing sudden stability issues that need further investigation.

    Windows Reliability Monitor is an easy application to use, although accessing the program itself can be a little tricky. Every version of Windows can access the program by opening the Run box (Windows Key + R) and typing in:.

    In a recent development, if you are using Windows 8 or later, you can also find the Reliability Monitor by opening the Start menu and typing in "reliability." You should see "View reliability history" as an option. Click on it to bring up the Reliability Monitor. The Control Panel is a third way to access the Reliability Monitor, located under the "Security and Maintenance" subsection of the Security tab.

    The application itself is easy to understand. You'll see a grid of events that break down your system's stability based on event logs. Windows keeps track of hardware and application performance at all times, so if something goes wrong, it creates an event log entry that shows up here.

    Industry observers note that clicking the blue "i" icons brings up information about your system that day, such as successful updates or software installations. Any days that experienced a critical software or hardware failure will have a red "x" icon next to them. Clicking the red icon will open the flagged events for further investigation. Days are also ranked with a stability score, indicating how long your PC has gone without issues. It's not the most reliable data point since you can easily inflate the score by not using your PC, but it can be a starting point when troubleshooting.

    While Windows Reliability Monitor doesn't directly improve performance, it can help you find applications and faulty drivers that are causing performance problems. For example, if you experience frequent GPU crashes while running certain applications, those problems would be logged as events and appear in Reliability Monitor. Inspecting the event provides information on what caused the crash, when it occurred and what applications were running at the time. This can help diagnose whether it's a hardware or software problem, giving you a clear path to fix the error and improve your system's stability and overall performance.

    If you are more focused on your system's performance, Windows offers the Performance Monitor tool to check your hardware's real-time usage. This is a better tool for diagnosing complications with a potentially faulty CPU, GPU, RAM, or network instability. Task Manager is also an invaluable tool for inspecting background applications that could be using your PC's resources.

    More experienced Windows users might wonder why they'd use the Reliability Monitor over the Event Viewer. For experienced PC users who want an exhaustive breakdown of each event log, the Event Viewer is unmatched. It offers significantly more information on each system event and has multiple ways to filter information to help pinpoint what's wrong.

    Industry observers note that where Reliability Monitor shines is its simplicity. It gives a clean UI to see which events caused an issue, when they occurred and a rough outline of what happened. Event Viewer can help if you need details on the exact application or your PC's state during failure, yet that information is often overkill for the average Windows user. If you need more information on the issue, then we'd suggest swapping to Event Viewer to get a better idea of what's happening. For sudden performance or stability issues, it's much more convenient to use Reliability Monitor first.

    The explosion ripped through one of the city's central squares.

    A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.

    The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.

    No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

    Recent findings suggest that colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details. Armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by De la Espriella.

    Writing on social media, the president said that his government would "bluntly and forcefully" respond, external to "every drop of Colombian blood spilled".

    "There will be no impunity and no retreat," he added.

    It is the latest in a series of attacks targeting official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

    Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province.

    And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of CÃºcuta.

    The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.

    Following the signing of the deal, thousands of left-wing rebel fighters laid down their arms.

    However, a significant number of Farc members, who did not agree with the deal, refused to disarm and joined dissident groups instead.

    While forced displacement, child recruitment and the numbers of attacks on security forces dropped in the aftermath of the deal, there has been an upsurge in recent years driven by dissident Farc factions and criminal groups fighting for control of drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion rackets.

    Colombia's first left-wing president, who was in power from August 2022 to August 2026, tried to negotiate with these armed groups as part of what he called his "total peace" strategy.

    However, the talks stalled and collapsed with several of the criminal groups violating ceasefires they had agreed to observe.

    De la Espriella was elected on a promise to crack down on "narcoterrorism" and has been scathing about his predecessor's approach.

    He has also been critical of the 2016 agreement, calling it a "false peace".

    In a post on X, uploaded shortly before news of the car bomb in Villavicencio spread, he referred to the peace deal as a "mess", describing it as a "waste of public resources" and the "cause behind Colombia's ruin".

    Former President Juan Manuel Santos and Rodrigo LondoÃ±o - the two men who signed the peace deal on behalf of the Colombian government and the Farc respectively - defended it in an interview with BBC Mundo ahead of the anniversary.

    Santos mentioned that De la Espriella was "totally wrong" to call it a "false peace".

    "He wants to use, or has bought into that cynical and mistaken theory that the violence we see today is the result of the peace deal, when the exact opposite is the case," Santos mentioned, arguing that the problem lies with the lack of implementation of the agreement.

    #81602. Industry News: Researchers find 3.6 billion usernames, passwords and documents in unsecured databases

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (622 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Researchers find 3.6 billion usernames, passwords and documents in unsecured databases

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The scale of the exposed data underscores how important it is to take steps to stay safe online.
    • Sources indicate that security researchers have unearthed two unsecured databases containing more than 3.6 billion records, including usernames, passwords, documents and national identity numbers.
    • In a recent development, he stated the database contains hundreds of millions of email accounts, north of 100 million social media accounts and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The scale of the exposed data underscores how important it is to take steps to stay safe online.

    Sources indicate that security researchers have unearthed two unsecured databases containing more than 3.6 billion records, including usernames, passwords, documents and national identity numbers. Wired reported that Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler found one of the databases, which contains roughly 2 billion login credentials. Fowler stated they were "associated with virtually every type of online service imaginable.".

    In a recent development, he stated the database contains hundreds of millions of email accounts, north of 100 million social media accounts and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts. It's estimated to include more than 114 million accounts linked to Google services, 88 million Facebook accounts, nearly 33 million X accounts, almost 42 million Roblox accounts and 36.6 million Amazon accounts, though Fowler indicated there may be some overlap between services and/or individual consumers.

    The database is noted to feature thousands of folders with plaintext credentials and account details. Dozens of countries were specified in the folder names, including the US, UK, France and Germany. There were also about 400,000 documents that "appeared to come from more advanced malware that created separate folders for individual victims," according to Fowler.

    Industry observers note that the other database reportedly contains north of 1.6 billion documents, primarily relating to people and businesses in China. It's said to include at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, approximately 11 million student enrollment records (many of which were for minors) and 7.8 million business registrations.

    According to recent reports, greg Pollock, security manufacturer UpGuard's director of research, found the database on the public internet on what appeared to be a gray market framework. Pollock told Wired the database was updated as recently as a week before he spotted it in October.

    It has been revealed that both databases — which have been removed from where the researchers found them — collated information from multiple sources, according to the report. The larger database is said to include data procured by infostealer malware that can harvest all login credentials from a single device, along with information obtained from elsewhere.

    In a recent development, as for the China-focused database, "the data comes from sources controlled by entirely separate authorities: ID registration (the Ministry of Public Security), payment app data (Ant Group, a private manufacturer), student enrollment (the education system) and business registration (market regulators)," Pollock wrote in a blog post. "No single lawful holder could legally possess all of them. The underlying records almost certainly originated in real government, telecom and corporate systems. What this server represents is the assembly of that stolen material into a working product.".

    At this point, it's reasonable to assume that some of your private data is out there. Data breaches, unfortunately, happen all the time — I've been notified about at least three that have impacted me and my information in the last month. The proliferation of AI is making it easier for attackers to find system vulnerabilities, gain access to a firm's or organization's servers and make off with data. AI can help them collate disparate information into databases such as these too.

    Still, there are measures you can take to help protect yourself and your data. Having strong, unique passwords for every single service you use is absolutely vital. A password manager can help you juggle all of those. Passkeys, multi-factor authentication and a good VPN are very useful too. Being more judicious about what information you share and with which services should stand you in better stead, as will being vigilant for social engineering and phishing attacks. Data removal services can come in handy as well.

    • To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that it took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.

    "Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this.".

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That issue is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.

    It has been revealed that after the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?".

    There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.

    NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members currently lack unanimity on this matter. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte mentioned.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz noted at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.

    Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these problems might come up again.".

    The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

    Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he noted weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply.".

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    It has been revealed that the contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).

    It has been revealed that the Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer stated. Also, a much larger one than before. "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness.".

    Sources indicate that following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who highlighted keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's upcoming post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer stated.

    This article was originally written in German.

    Tidal confirms ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them.
    • Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI.
    • As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the firm is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.

    Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of newly introduced uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.

    As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.

    Credit: Tidal Credit: Tidal.

    Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an issue with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal states it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this enhancement.

    According to recent reports, as of December 9, individual uploaders and distributors will no longer be allowed to add AI music to Tidal. However, they could lie, couldn’t they?

    Tidal hasn’t specified how it detects AI music, but it will probably rely on watermarking. Almost every AI song on Tidal (94 percent) comes from Suno, which added watermarking earlier this year. Tidal also cites Google Lyria as a source of AI tunes, which has SynthID labels embedded in the waveform. Deezer claimed it has a licensable AI music detector with a false-positive rate of less than 0.01 percent, but it’s unclear if Tidal is using that or something similar.

    Recent findings suggest that that will take care of most AI music, but this approach won’t detect everything. There are open models for music generation that you can run locally on a GPU, and some cloud-based providers aren’t bothering to watermark their outputs. Even if Tidal is using a separate detection system, new models may be able to evade it—it’s always going to be a cat-and-mouse game. This will be a problem with verifying provenance in all types of media in the future. For the time being, at least, Tidal’s policy should clear out most of the AI slop.

    According to recent reports, the people directing robots to make these songs will have plenty of other options after Tidal blocks AI. Spotify, YouTube Music, Deezer, and Apple Music all allow AI music on their platforms with labeling. Spotify has removed millions of AI tracks from its collection based on user feedback. Other streamers haven’t specified how much slop (if any) they’ve cleared out.
